title: An option or preference value that carries a path is a file-write primitive inside the directory you meant to protect
index_line: T-0037 · FILE_WRITE · a transcoder flag takes an output path; the write lands in the directory the process loads code from · c/any-child-process · corroborated
invariant_violated: A setting is assumed to configure *how* a job runs, so it is validated as an enum-ish string. But some of those settings are file paths by nature — output directory, log target, cache location — and the child process writes exactly where it is told. No traversal is needed: the write lands in a directory the application itself loads code from.

mechanism.does: the attacker obtains a privileged session (here via an SSRF→loopback-only-API→token chain) and reaches the settings surface
a preference that takes an output path is set to a directory the process will later load code from (a codec/plugin directory)
a transcode is started against an attacker-hosted input, so the child process decodes attacker-chosen content into attacker-chosen frames
the decoder writes its output to the configured path, creating a file with attacker-controlled bytes inside a trusted directory
the next start of the service loads code from that directory, so the written file is executed rather than read

source.http.request.value: the preference/settings and transcode-start requests; the interesting field is the one that names a directory, not the one that names an option

sink.file.write.value: the child process's output write — the write is the feature, and the destination is the payload

fs.path.join.value: the configured directory joined with the generated filename; both halves are attacker-influenced

encoding.url.value: the SSRF/URL-confusion step that gets you a privileged session in the first place (`127.0.0.1.<attacker>` prefix trust, alt-IP forms)

guard.none.value: no check that an output path stays out of the directories the process loads code from

preconditions.expr: a settings surface is writable by a role reachable by the attacker (admin, or whatever the chain yields)
a preference value that is joined with a filename and used as an output directory by a child process
a directory the process loads executable code from is writable by that process

check.spec: ls -ld Codecs/ plugins/ lib/ 2>/dev/null; lsof -p $(pgrep -f 'the service') 2>/dev/null | grep -E '\.so|\.dll' | head

success: a new file appears in a code-loading directory, with content derived from attacker-supplied media rather than from the application
the write happens during a normal transcode/export, so no upload endpoint is needed
the file is loaded on the next service start
failure_like: output paths are confined to a scratch directory, or the child is run in a sandbox with the code directories read-only
the preference value is validated against an enum or a restricted character set rather than accepted as a path
false_positive: a file created in the output directory by a legitimate export — check the directory is one the process *loads* from
a transcode that merely fails: the write may still have happened, so verify on disk rather than by response

hazards: the interesting question is not 'is this field injectable' but 'what does the child process *write*, and where does it load from'
the initial access is usually a different bug — record the write primitive separately so it can be chained with whatever gets you privileges
bit-exact output (frame dumps, core dumps, cache blobs) makes the written file attacker-controlled byte for byte; do not assume an encoder sanitises it
admin-only CVSS understates this class: the admin role exists to configure the service, and configuring it into code execution is a boundary failure
non_transfers: export paths fixed to a scratch directory the loader never reads
services whose code directories are read-only at runtime
